actionable-error.definition: A tool result that says what went wrong and what to do next, in few words.

additional-properties.definition: A schema setting. Set to false, it refuses a field the schema does not name. This course's checker refuses it.

agent.definition: A model that is called in a loop, asks for tools, and is stopped by the code around it. The model is one part of the agent.

agent-computer-interface.definition: The tools as a model sees them: their names, descriptions, inputs and results. It is a user interface for the model.

agent-loop.definition: The code that calls the model, runs the tools the model asks for, adds the results to the history, and calls the model again. It stops when one of its exits is taken.

agents-md.definition: A rules file in the repository, named by a convention. Which product reads it is a fact the course lists, not a claim made here.

agreement-rate.definition: The share of cases where a grader and a human give the same verdict. It does not say which way the errors fall.

allow.definition: A decision that lets a tool call run without asking anyone.

allow-list.definition: A list of commands or tools that may run without asking. Naming a command is not enough on its own: its target still matters.

altitude.definition: How specific an instruction is. Too low and it is a lookup table; too high and it is a slogan. Good instructions are specific enough to act on and general enough to transfer.

append-only-history.definition: A history that only grows at the end. Earlier messages are never changed or removed.

applied-ai-engineer.definition: A job title for an engineer who builds agents into a product, with tools, evals and guardrails. In this course's terms it is most of the work the course teaches.

approval-fatigue.definition: The loss of care that follows many prompts, so that the one dangerous prompt is approved without a look.

approval-mode.definition: A setting that decides which actions wait for a person before they run, and which run on their own.

ask.definition: A decision that sends the call to a person before it runs. Asking is a cost: every prompt is a chance to approve by habit.

attack-success-rate.definition: The share of seeded attack runs in which the attack succeeded. Report it with the number of runs it came from.

attention-budget.definition: The limited capacity of a model to draw on a large context when it reads it.

auto-mode.definition: In Claude Code, auto is a permission mode that lets everything run without asking, with background safety checks.

batch-processing.definition: Sending many requests as one job, to be answered later rather than at once. It trades the wait for a different price.

blast-radius.definition: How much a single mistake can reach: the files, the network and the secrets it could touch.

brag-sheet.definition: A one-page print of your readiness: your levels, the modules you explained, your passed katas and steps, your bench results, your design drills and the date. It lists only what your evidence shows.

brain.definition: The model and its loop: it reads the history, decides the next call, and keeps the credentials.

breaking-change.definition: A change that makes working code fail, or behave differently, without any change on your side.

brief.definition: The message a sub-agent starts from: the task, the files it may read, and the fields its result must return.

budget-guard.definition: A check that stops a run when its token or cost budget is spent, and keeps the trace of what it did.

build-to-delete.definition: Write a harness part so it can be removed when a newer model no longer needs it, and measure before you remove it.

cache-breakpoint.definition: The point up to which a request asks to be cached. The course's model of caching uses one, at the end of the request.

cache-hit.definition: A call that reads some of its input from the cache. The hit rate is the share of the input that was read.

cache-invalidation.definition: A change that makes earlier cache entries stop matching, so the next call writes the request again.

cache-prefix.definition: The part of a request that comes before a point. A cache matches a prefix whole, or not at all.

cache-read.definition: Input that a call takes from the cache instead of processing it again.

cache-ttl.definition: How long a cache entry lasts after it was last written or read.

cache-write.definition: Input that a call stores in the cache, so that a later call can read it.

calibration.definition: Checking a grader against human labels you trust, and measuring how often the two agree and which way the grader errs.

canary.definition: A small share of real traffic sent to a new harness, to see its behaviour before a wider rollout.

capability-check.definition: A check of the model's profile before a request is sent. It drops or refuses the parameters the model rejects.

capability-eval.definition: An eval that asks what the agent can do yet. Its pass rate should climb as the harness improves.

checkpoint.definition: A saved record of what is done and what the next step is, written after each step.

circuit-breaker.definition: A switch that opens after a set number of failures in a row, and holds calls back for a cooldown.

claude-md.definition: A rules file in the repository, named by a convention. Which product reads it is a fact the course lists, not a claim made here.

clean-reset.definition: Starting a new run with only the task and a handoff note, instead of compacting the old one.

code-grader.definition: A program that decides. A run passes when it ends done and the tape's checks hold. It cannot be talked into a pass.

code-tour.definition: A fixed order for reading an unfamiliar harness: the loop, the model adapter, the tools, the config, then the trace.

commit.definition: One saved change, with a message that says what it does. This course asks for small commits, each one explainable in a line.

compaction.definition: Replacing the older messages with a summary, so the desk has room again. The summary keeps only what the harness chose to keep.

compaction-threshold.definition: The share of the window at which a compaction runs. A low threshold compacts often; a high one lets the desk fill.

compounding-error.definition: When each step can fail, the chance that all the steps succeed falls with every step.

computational-check.definition: A check a program can run and decide: tests, linters and type checks. Its answer does not depend on who asks.

concurrency.definition: Doing more than one thing in the same period, so that a program does other work while it waits.

confidence-interval.definition: A range the true rate is likely to lie in, given the trials. Its width shrinks as the trials grow.

constrained-decoding.definition: Generating a reply so that only the tokens a schema allows can be chosen. A method, compared in this module.

container.definition: A process with its own smaller view of the machine. The course treats it as one wall among others, not as the whole of the wall.

contamination.definition: A test case the model saw while it learned or while you tuned. The score then measures memory, not the task.

content-block.definition: One typed part of a response: text, or a tool request. Each block has a type that says what fields it has.

context-budget.definition: The share of the window that each part of the desk takes, counted before the model sees any of it.

context-engineering.definition: Choosing what goes on the desk for each call, and what gets cut or saved.

context-management.definition: The wire that answers what is on the desk this call, and what is saved.

context-rot.definition: The fall in answer quality as the window fills, well before the hard limit is reached.

context-window.definition: The fixed-size desk the model reads on each call. Instructions, earlier messages, tool results and the reply all share it.

control-plane.definition: The wire that answers what the model is told, and which instruction wins.

conversation-history.definition: The earlier messages in the list. The harness keeps them, and decides how much of them each call sends.

coroutine.definition: What an async def function returns when you call it.

cost-attribution.definition: Splitting a model call's cost into its parts, and naming the largest part of the request.

cost-per-completed-task.definition: The cost of a task's calls, divided by the share of tasks that finish. A cheap call that often fails is not cheap.

dataclass.definition: A Python class that holds named fields. The @dataclass decorator writes the __init__ method, so Rein can build a reply with named fields.

decision-order.definition: The fixed order a policy is checked in: all deny rules, then all ask rules, then all allow rules, then the mode's default.

defense-in-depth.definition: Several controls, each stopping something different, so that one control failing does not decide the outcome.

deferred-loading.definition: Keeping a tool's definition out of the request until a step needs it.

deny.definition: A decision that stops the tool call. It runs nothing, and the model gets the reason.

deprecation.definition: A notice that a parameter or format still works but will be removed, so code should move before it is.

destructive-tool.definition: A tool that may change or delete things in its environment.

determinism.definition: The same inputs and seeds give the same run, so a result can be reproduced.

diff.definition: The text that shows which lines a change adds, removes or leaves alone, file by file.

done-claim.definition: The model's own statement that it has finished, carried by end_turn. The loop treats it as a claim to check. It is not proof that the task is done.

drift.definition: Slow change in what a model does over time, so that a result that worked stops working without any change in the harness.

durable-execution.definition: A run whose progress is kept outside the process, so a crash does not lose it.

edit-file.definition: A tool that replaces one exact piece of text in a file. The text must appear exactly once, so the edit is unambiguous.

effort.definition: A setting that tells the model how much to work before it answers. The harness sets it on each request.

egress-allow-list.definition: The hosts a network call may reach. A call to any other host is refused.

end-turn.definition: The stop reason for a response that finished on its own. It is a done claim, not proof.

entropy.definition: The slow drift of a codebase and its rules away from each other, as code changes and the map stays where it was.

enum.definition: A field that may take only one of a short list of values.

environment.definition: The files, tools and board a task runs in. It stays fixed, so two runs differ only by the change under test.

eval.definition: A fixed set of tasks, run over seeded trials and graded, with a count of the passes. A harness change is judged by it.

eval-awareness.definition: A model that suspects it is being tested and may behave differently. The course treats it as a principle to design against.

evals-engineer.definition: A job title for an engineer who designs the tasks, scoring checks and experiments that measure an agent, and reads the noise in its results.

evaluator.definition: The role that grades each step against criteria written outside the generator's own work.

event.definition: One record the harness writes as it runs: a model call, a tool call, a permission decision. Each has a sequence number and a time.

event-log.definition: A record of every turn, call and result of a run. Nothing in it is edited or removed.

excessive-agency.definition: An agent that can do more than its task needs, so that a mistake or a manipulated output can do damage.

exfiltration.definition: A secret leaving the sandbox through a network call.

exit.definition: A reason the loop stops. A loop with one exit stops only when that one exit is taken.

exponential-backoff.definition: Waiting longer after each failed try, doubling the wait each time up to a cap.

extended-thinking.definition: Extra tokens the model writes before it answers, to work a problem out. The thinking is billed as output.

fail-closed.definition: When a check cannot decide, it denies the action. A check that fails open lets the action through when it breaks.

failure-family.definition: A named kind of failure that recurs across runs, such as a false done. Each module teaches one family.

failure-mode.definition: A way a model's answer can go wrong. The course names six that a harness has to plan for.

fakemodel.definition: The scripted model in Rein. It answers from a fixed list, so every run repeats exactly and needs no key and no network.

fan-out.definition: Starting several sub-agents at once, one per piece of work, and reading their results together.

feature-list.definition: A file of the work the task needs, each item marked done or not, so a session can see what is left without guessing.

file-permissions.definition: The rules that say which user may read, write or run a file, given its owner, its group and its mode.

final-status.definition: The one word that says how a run ended, such as done, max turns, interrupted or error.

fixture.definition: A helper that builds the setup a test needs, so each test starts from the same known state.

forked-context.definition: A sub-agent that starts from the parent's messages so far, plus its brief. It knows more, and its first request is larger.

forward-deployed-engineer.definition: A job title for an engineer who fits an agent into a customer's codebase and workflow, often working with the customer directly.

framework.definition: A library of ready-made parts for building a harness. It supplies parts; it does not decide your harness for you.

function-calling.definition: Another name for a tool call: the model writes a structured request for a named function with its arguments.

gate.definition: The check every tool call passes before it runs. It returns allow, ask or deny, with a reason the model can read.

genai-conventions.definition: OpenTelemetry's names for generative AI spans and attributes. The registry declares them in development, so names can still change.

generator.definition: The role that does the work of each step and hands its output to the evaluator.

golden-set.definition: A small set of cases with human labels you trust, kept to calibrate a grader against.

grader.definition: The check that says whether a run passed. Every eval has one, and it can be wrong in its own way.

ground-truth.definition: A check that does not depend on the model's words: a test, a file, a number that can be looked up.

guard.definition: A check that ends a run for a reason the harness can name: the turn limit, the token budget, or a call repeated after it was redirected. Each guard writes a guard line, then ends the run with its own status.

guide.definition: A control that steers the model before the work, such as a rule in the prompt or a template.

hallucination.definition: A fluent, specific claim that is false. The reply reads the same as a true one, so reading it does not reveal the error.

handoff-note.definition: A short written record of the goal, the constraints, the decisions, the progress and the files, that a new run reads first.

hands.definition: The sandboxes and tools that act on the workspace. They run what the brain asks for.

harness.definition: Everything around the model: the loop, the tools, the permissions, the checks and the limits. Same model, different harness, different results.

harness-board.definition: The harness's settings, such as limits and gates, shown next to what a run does.

harness-engineering.definition: Building and tuning the code around the model: the loop, tools, permissions, checks and limits.

harnessable-codebase.definition: A codebase with fast checks, clear errors, a readable structure and docs that work as a map.

header.definition: A named line of metadata in an HTTP request or response, such as a content type or a retry-after value, sent before the body.

hidden-tests.definition: Tests the policy cannot read or edit. They check the work on inputs the workspace does not show.

hook.definition: Code the harness runs at a fixed point, such as before a tool call, so the rule holds whatever the prompt says.

http-status-code.definition: The three-digit number in an HTTP response that says what happened to the request, such as 200 or 429.

human-grader.definition: A person who reads a run and gives a verdict. A careful person is slow, and two people can disagree.

human-in-the-loop.definition: A step that waits for a person to approve it before it runs, with the step shown in words they can check.

idempotency.definition: A property of an action: doing it again with the same request has the same effect as doing it once.

idempotency-key.definition: A value sent with a request, so that a repeated request can be recognised and not run twice.

image.definition: The name of the starting point a container runs from, such as python:3.

independent-reviewer.definition: A reviewer that sees the task and the diff, not the author's reasoning, so it judges the result and not the story.

indirect-prompt-injection.definition: A prompt injection that arrives through content the agent fetched. The person typing never wrote it.

inference.definition: A model call that reads the weights and the prompt and produces a reply. The weights stay the same during inference.

inferential-check.definition: A check that judges with a model or a person: a review of the code or of the claim. Useful where no program can decide.

infrastructure-noise.definition: Variation from the machine, the network or a time limit, rather than from the model or the change.

initializer-agent.definition: The first session of a long task. It sets up the files, a feature list and a progress file, so later sessions start from a known state.

input-schema.definition: The part of a tool definition that says which fields the tool takes, their types, and which fields are required.

input-tokens.definition: The tokens the model reads on a call: the instructions, the earlier messages, the tool results and the new message.

instruction-hierarchy.definition: The order that decides which layer wins when two of them disagree. It is set by who wrote each layer, not by what it says.

instruction-layer.definition: One block of text in the prompt that tells the model what to do: the system prompt, the project rules, the user's message or a tool result.

interrupt.definition: A stop that a person asks for while a run is going. The harness must still answer what the run had started.

is-error.definition: An optional field of a tool_result. It is set to true when the tool call failed, and says so to the model.

isolated-context.definition: A sub-agent that starts from its brief alone. It cannot see the parent's messages, so its first request is small.

jitter.definition: A random part of the wait, so that many clients that failed together do not retry together.

json-schema.definition: A way to write down the shape of a JSON object: its fields, their types, which are required and which values are allowed.

jsonl.definition: JSON Lines: one JSON object per line. Each line is written as its event happens, so every line written so far is complete.

just-in-time-retrieval.definition: Loading a piece of material when the task needs it, instead of loading everything at the start.

language-model.definition: A model that reads a text and scores the possible next tokens. A harness calls it again and again, and each call gives one reply.

latency.definition: How long a call takes to finish. More tokens in and out usually mean a longer wait.

latency-budget.definition: A limit on how long a task may take from start to end, set before you measure the work.

least-privilege.definition: Give a tool or an agent only the tools, paths and hosts its task needs. Refuse the rest by default.

lethal-trifecta.definition: Three legs together: the agent can read private data, it reads untrusted content, and it can send data out. With all three open, an injected instruction can steal data.

llm-judge.definition: A model that grades another model's run. The same as a model grader: cheap and quick, and it reads the claim as easily as the work.

long-running-agent.definition: An agent whose task spans more sessions than one context window holds. It needs a record of its state to carry on.

loop-detection.definition: Noticing that the run repeats the same action, and stopping it before the turn limit does.

managed-agent.definition: A run of an agent that someone else hosts, split into a brain, hands and an event log.

max-tokens.definition: The stop reason for a response that hit the request's length limit. The reply may be cut off in the middle.

mcp-client.definition: The part of a host that keeps one connection to one server. This is the course's model; the facts registry defines no client role.

mcp-host.definition: The application the user runs. It decides which servers to connect to. This is the course's model; the facts registry defines no host role.

mcp-resource.definition: Data that a server offers for the model to read, such as a file or a record.

mcp-server.definition: A program that offers tools, resources or prompts to a client.

memory.definition: Anything a run can use later: what is in the window, what is in saved files, or what is in the model's weights.

memory-file.definition: A file in the project that holds standing facts, read by every run in that project.

memory-tier.definition: One of the four places a harness keeps what a model needs: the window, the session log, the project files and the long-term store.

messages-api.definition: The API this course calls for every model call. A3 showed what each request holds.

messages-array.definition: The ordered list of messages sent with each call. It is the conversation the model can see.

migration-guide.definition: A list a vendor publishes of what changed between models. Read it for the changes that break your code.

mock-interview.definition: A practice interview in which someone else asks the questions and grades your answers against a rubric. You write down what to improve afterwards.

model-context-protocol.definition: An open protocol through which an application connects a model to tools, resources and prompts that other programs offer.

model-grader.definition: A judge model that reads a run and gives a verdict. It can pass a claim it never checked.

model-id.definition: The name that picks the model in a request. A run's trace records it.

model-interface.definition: One function that Rein calls to get a reply. A scripted model and a real model both sit behind it, with the same inputs and the same kind of result.

model-migration.definition: The work of moving a harness from one model to another, and checking that its assumptions still hold.

model-routing.definition: Choosing a model for each task, a cheap one for easy work and a capable one for hard work, from a rule or a check.

mount.definition: A folder you name in the command so the command can use it. This course mounts one folder per task.

nested-schema.definition: A schema whose properties are schemas themselves, so the check goes into the value one level at a time.

network-egress.definition: A network call that leaves the machine, to a host outside the sandbox.

next-token-prediction.definition: The model's one job on each step: score every possible next token. Nothing in this step checks whether a token is true.

observability.definition: The wire that answers what exactly happened, and where time and money went.

opentelemetry.definition: An open standard for traces, metrics and logs. This course takes its names for spans and attributes.

orchestrator.definition: The parent agent that starts sub-agents, gives each one a brief, and reads what they return.

orphaned-tool-call.definition: A tool call with no result after it. A request that holds one is refused.

outcome.definition: How a run ended: done, stopped by a limit, or failed, with the checks' verdict beside it.

output-cap.definition: A limit on how much of one tool output the model sees. It keeps the start and the end, and says how much was cut.

output-limit.definition: The most tokens one reply may use. A reply that reaches it stops there, and the reply says why.

output-tokens.definition: The tokens the model writes in its reply. They use the same window as the input.

overloaded-error.definition: The error the API returns when it is temporarily overloaded. It is a transient error.

parallel-safe.definition: Two tool calls are parallel-safe when neither writes a resource that the other reads or writes.

parallel-tool-calls.definition: Several tool_use blocks in one reply, so the harness runs them together and answers all of them in one message.

parametrize.definition: Running one test body over a table of cases, so each case is checked on its own.

pass-at-k.definition: The chance that at least one of k tries passes. It shows what a harness can reach when it may retry.

pass-hat-k.definition: The chance that all k tries pass. It shows how reliable a single try is.

pass-rate.definition: The share of trials that pass their checks. It is a measure over many runs, not the result of one.

path-traversal.definition: A path that climbs out of the workspace root with ../, or that names a link leading out of it.

pause-and-resume.definition: Saving the run state, stopping, and later starting again from the saved state instead of from the beginning.

pause-turn.definition: The stop reason for a server-side loop that reached its iteration limit. The harness decides whether to continue.

permanent-error.definition: A failure that will repeat on every try, such as a request that is badly formed. A retry does not help.

permission-mode.definition: The default decision for a call that no rule matches: allow, ask or deny.

permission-policy.definition: The rules that decide, for each tool call, whether it runs, asks a person, or is denied, written down as code.

permissions.definition: The wire that answers which actions are allowed, and how bad a mistake can get.

plan-mode.definition: In Claude Code, plan mode is a permission mode: Claude explores and writes a plan, and does not edit the source until the plan is approved, except in interactive terminal sessions with bypass permissions available.

planner.definition: The role that splits a task into steps and writes the order they run in. It hands the steps to the generator.

policy.definition: The model's behaviour in an environment: the actions it takes from what it sees. In this course a scripted policy stands in for a model.

pre-tool-hook.definition: A hook that runs before each tool call and decides whether the call may run.

probability.definition: A number from zero to one that says how likely a choice is. The sampler turns the scores into probabilities before it picks.

process.definition: A running program, with its own id, its parent's id, a user and a working folder.

product-harness.definition: The harness a vendor ships with its model product, with its own loop, tools and limits.

programmatic-tool-calling.definition: The model writes a short program that calls several tools, so that only the program's result returns to the context. The idea only; the course makes no product claim.

progress-file.definition: A file the sessions write and read: what is done, what is next and what is open. The harness can pass it into the next session.

progressive-disclosure.definition: Loading detail only when a task needs it: the short description first, the full procedure when it is used.

project-rules.definition: The standing instructions for one repository, written down so every run in it reads them.

prompt-caching.definition: Keeping the start of a request, so that a later call with the same start can read it back instead of processing it again.

prompt-engineering.definition: Choosing the words of the prompt and the instructions. Words guide the model; they do not enforce anything.

prompt-injection.definition: Instructions hidden in content the agent reads: a page, a file, a tool's output. The model may act on them as if a person had asked.

queue.definition: A line of work that waits its turn, so the run keeps its order when the provider is busy.

race-condition.definition: A bug where the result depends on which of two steps runs first.

randomness.definition: The model can give different answers to the same prompt. One good run says little about the next.

rate-limit.definition: A cap on how many requests or tokens a client may use in a period. Going over it returns an error.

react.definition: A name for the loop of reasoning and acting in turns, from the paper ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.

read-only-tool.definition: A tool that does not change its environment. A read-only hint says so; it is still a hint.

readiness-level.definition: One of three levels on a wire's row of the readiness radar: can explain (L1), have built (L2) and can defend with data (L3). Each level needs the one below it, and each comes from entries in your evidence.

recovery.definition: The wire that answers how a failure is handled, so the run continues without spinning.

red-teaming.definition: Attacking your own agent on purpose, with a fixed set of attacks, to find what it lets through.

redaction.definition: Replacing secret text with a placeholder before the event is stored. It changes the trace, not what the model is sent.

refusal.definition: The stop reason for a response where the model declined to answer. It arrives as a normal reply, not an error.

regression-eval.definition: An eval that guards what already works. Its pass rate should hold, and a drop is the news.

rein.definition: The small agent harness you build one step at a time. Each step adds a few lines, then a checkpoint compares your output with the expected output.

reinforcement-learning.definition: Training a model by letting it try actions in an environment and adjusting it toward the actions that earn more reward.

reliability.definition: How often a task works all the way through. In this course it comes from the system around the model.

request.definition: What the harness sends for one model call: the system prompt, the tools and the messages.

research-engineer.definition: A job title for an engineer who builds the environments, sandboxes and scoring checks that measure and train models.

reset.definition: Returning an environment to its starting state, so the next run begins from the same workspace and seeds.

response.definition: What the model sends back for one call: a list of content blocks and a stop reason.

retry-budget.definition: A limit on the retries a run or a client may make, so that retries cannot grow without end.

reward.definition: The number a grader gives a run. A training loop learns from it, and it can differ from whether the task was really solved.

reward-hacking.definition: A run that earns the reward without solving the task, for example by editing the test that grades it.

rl-environment.definition: The tasks, sandbox, tools, grader and reward that a policy is trained or tested in.

role.definition: The label on each message in the list. A message is from the user or from the assistant.

rollout.definition: Widening the share of traffic that a new harness gets, one step at a time, each step gated by its evals.

rules-file.definition: A file that holds the project rules. Kept short, it is a map of where things are and how to check them.

run.definition: One agent doing one task, from the first model call to a stop. A run has many turns.

run-command.definition: A tool that runs a shell command in the project folder and returns its exit code and output, with a time limit.

run-state.definition: Everything a run remembers between calls: its messages, its turn count and its status. The harness keeps it in one place.

sample-size.definition: The number of trials behind a rate. It moves the interval more than the point estimate does.

sampling.definition: The step that picks one token from the scored options, by the rules it is given. The model scores; the sampler picks.

sandbox.definition: The limit on where an action can reach, such as files and the network.

sandbox-first.definition: A design where every tool call runs inside a confined environment, and the confinement is set before the first call.

scenario-tape.definition: A JSON file that lists the scripted replies one run uses. The --fake flag points Rein at it.

schema-validation.definition: Checking a value against a schema before the harness uses it. The checker returns the first reason the value fails.

secret.definition: A value that must not reach the model's reply or the trace, such as an API key.

seed.definition: The number that sets the random draws of a scripted run. The same seed gives the same run, every time.

self-praise.definition: A model saying its work is good when it is not. A model checking its own work has the same blind spots.

self-report.definition: The model's own statement about its work, such as "the tests pass". A self-report is a claim until a check confirms it.

self-tuning-harness.definition: A harness that adjusts one of its settings from measured runs, and only after a person has agreed the measure.

sensor.definition: A control that checks after the work, such as a test run, a linter or a review of the diff.

server-sent-events.definition: The name for the events in a stream. This course shows them as plain Python dictionaries.

session.definition: One run of the harness on a task, from its first request to its end. A new session starts with what the harness sends it.

session-log.definition: A record of one session's events, kept so a later session or a reader can see what happened.

shadow-mode.definition: Running a new harness beside the old one, comparing the results, and letting only the old one act.

skill.definition: A folder with a SKILL.md file: a short description, and the procedure for one kind of task.

skill-md.definition: The file in a skill's folder: YAML frontmatter followed by the procedure in Markdown.

span.definition: A timed piece of work in a trace: a name, a start, an end, its attributes, and the span it sits under.

stale-knowledge.definition: Facts the model holds that have changed since it learned them. The model does not know they are out of date.

stateless.definition: Keeping nothing between calls. A stateless call starts from what it is sent, and nothing else.

steering-loop.definition: Watch the runs, name the failure family, fix the harness, then measure the fix.

stop-reason.definition: The field in every response that says why the model stopped: end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens and a few others.

streaming.definition: Receiving a reply as a sequence of events, instead of one whole response. The events build the same message.

structured-output.definition: A reply in a shape you asked for, such as a JSON object with named fields. It is still a model's reply: the shape can be right and the values wrong.

sub-agent.definition: A second agent run by the harness for one job, such as review. It is a separate run, with its own context.

supply-chain.definition: The servers, packages and versions a harness depends on. Each one can change without the harness changing.

symlink.definition: A file that names another path. In this course's sandbox, a link's target is relative to the link's own folder, and the sandbox follows it.

system-design-interview.definition: A session in which you design a system out loud with an interviewer, and are judged on the decisions and trade-offs, not on a single right answer.

system-prompt.definition: The instructions sent with every call, kept apart from the messages. The harness sends it each time.

taint.definition: A value that came from untrusted content and keeps that origin. A tainted value should not decide an action that sends data out.

take-home.definition: A small project with a fixed brief and time limit, done alone and written up for review.

task.definition: One thing you ask the agent to do, with its starting files and what counts as done.

temperature.definition: A setting of the sampler that changes how much the scores count. Higher temperature spreads the choice over more tokens. At zero, the top token always wins.

test-tampering.definition: Changing the tests so that they pass for the wrong reason: editing an assertion, clearing a marker, or special-casing the answer.

text-block.definition: A content block of type text. It holds words, and no tool request.

thinking-block.definition: The part of a reply that holds the model's thinking. In a tool loop, it goes back to the model unchanged with the tool call.

time-to-first-token.definition: The wait from sending a request to the first token of the reply. It is latency, not how fast the model writes.

token.definition: A piece of text the model reads and writes. A token is often a word, but it can be part of a word or a punctuation mark.

token-bucket.definition: A limit that fills at a steady rate. Each call takes one token, and an empty bucket means wait.

token-budget.definition: A cap on the total tokens a run may use, input and output together. The loop checks it before each call and stops when the total has reached the cap.

token-estimate.definition: A rough count of a request's size, at about four characters per token, used to decide when to act. It is an estimate, not the provider's count.

tokenizer.definition: The part that cuts text into tokens. Real tokenizers differ, so a count from the course is an estimate.

tool.definition: A function the harness runs when the model asks for it. The model only asks. The harness runs the function and returns the result.

tool-annotation.definition: A hint a tool server gives about a tool, such as read-only or destructive. A hint is not a check.

tool-definition.definition: The name, the description and the input schema that tell the model a tool exists and what to pass it.

tool-description.definition: The text that tells the model what a tool does and when to use it. The model reads it on every call.

tool-poisoning.definition: A tool server changes what its tools say or do, so the model is steered by the change. The change can arrive in a new version of a server the harness already uses.

tool-registry.definition: A table from each tool name to the Python function that runs it. The loop looks up the name the model asked for. A name that is not in the table gets an error result.

tool-result.definition: The block that answers one tool_use. It carries the tool_use_id of the call and the output the harness got back.

tool-search.definition: Finding a tool's definition by keyword, and loading it for the next call. The course's simulator does it, and it makes no product claim.

tool-use.definition: A block in the model's reply that asks the harness to run a named tool with an input. The model writes it; the harness runs it.

tool-use-id.definition: The id of a tool_use block. A tool_result names the id of the call it answers.

topology.definition: The shape of a multi-agent system: who starts whom, who reads whose output, and where work waits.

trace.definition: The record of a run: each model call, reply, permission, tool call and check, in order.

trace-id.definition: The identifier that ties the spans and events of one run together, so one trace reads as one run.

training.definition: The process that sets the model's weights, from many example texts. It happens before any chat, and a chat does not run it.

trajectory.definition: The path a run took through its tools, step by step. Two runs can reach the same outcome by different paths.

transcript.definition: The record of one run: each model reply, tool call and result, in order.

transient-error.definition: A failure that is likely to pass on its own, such as a busy provider. A retry may succeed.

transport.definition: How messages move between a client and a server. Stdio uses newline-delimited messages over the standard streams of a subprocess.

trial.definition: One run with one seed. A bench runs many trials of the same setup.

turn.definition: One call to the model and the tool results that follow it. A run is a series of turns.

turn-clock.definition: The clock face that shows one turn of a run as eight wires in order, with the harness settings beside them.

turn-limit.definition: A cap on the number of model calls in one run. When the count reaches it, the loop stops.

type-hint.definition: A note that says what type a name should hold, such as count: int, or -> str after the parameters of a function.

untrusted-content.definition: Anything the agent reads that a stranger could have written: a page, a comment, a tool's answer. It is data, even when it is phrased as an order.

unverified.definition: A run status. The model said done, but the check still failed after the last fix round. The run ends as unverified, never as done.

usage.definition: The counts in a response: how many input and output tokens the call used. The cost of a call comes from them.

user-harness.definition: The harness you add around a model product or API: your loop, your tools and your checks.

variance.definition: How far a result moves from one batch of runs to the next. A pass rate from few trials has high variance.

verification.definition: The wire that answers whether a done claim is really done, and whether a change helped.

verification-gate.definition: The check that sits between the model's done claim and the run's success. A claim passes only when the gate runs and passes.

virtual-clock.definition: A clock that moves forward by the waits it is asked to sleep, without waiting in real time. A retry costs no time, so a test of backoff runs at once and repeats exactly.

virtual-environment.definition: A folder with its own Python packages, kept apart from the system's. The course's scripted run needs none; the real-model path installs one package.

virtual-machine.definition: A whole guest system that runs on a host. The course compares it with a container and an OS sandbox, by cost and by isolation.

weights.definition: The numbers inside the model that set its scores. Training sets them. Inference only reads them.

wilson-interval.definition: A confidence interval for a pass rate that stays inside 0 and 1 and stays honest at small counts.

wire.definition: One of the eight parts of a harness, and one spoke of the Turn Clock. Each wire answers one question about a turn.

workspace-root.definition: The folder the agent may use. A path that leaves it is outside the workspace.

worktree.definition: A separate folder for one line of work, so an agent's files stay apart from yours in this course's practice.

write-up.definition: A short document that states the question, the method, the command that reproduces the numbers, the results table and the limits. A reviewer should be able to run it and get the same numbers.
